name: Romantic nationalism
summary: Romantic nationalism holds that a people is a natural community of shared language, culture and history, that each such people has the right to govern itself in its own state within borders that follow the nation rather than dynasties, and that its culture is to be preserved and its spirit renewed. In the mainstream strand of Herder, Mazzini and Kossuth the cause is liberal, anti-conquest and consistent with duty to humanity; Fichte's strand adds a claim of German superiority. The sources mostly address the national question and a few connected moral claims, so most other statements are left blank.
scope: The national-question doctrine of the nineteenth-century romantic nationalists: Herder's cultural nation, Fichte's Addresses to the German Nation, Mazzini's Duties of Man and writings, Kossuth's speeches and Michelet's The People, with Herder's Ideen (Book 9), Arndt's Der Rhein and Catechism, Jahn's Deutsches Volksthum, the Grimms' preface to the Deutsche Sagen and Mickiewicz's Books of the Polish Nation. Their wider political, economic and social programmes are not taken as the doctrine's unless the nationalist texts state them as part of the national cause; the later racial and fascist nationalisms are excluded.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Herder's call to respect and preserve every people's culture, Fichte's national education and Mazzini's national mission all make the preservation of a people's own culture the movement's core aim.

national-self-determination.rationale: Mazzini says the map must be redrawn as countries of the peoples defined by the vote of free men, and Kossuth proclaims the sovereign right of every nation to dispose of itself.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Fichte, Mazzini and Arndt make a shared language the mark of a nation and Herder's nation is a linguistic one, but Kossuth rejects language as the basis of nationality and says a state divided by language would be ruined.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Mazzini says Europe's boundaries were disfigured by dynasties' conquests and will be redrawn along national lines, Fichte treats the language community as the natural state and Kossuth condemns the Habsburg partition of Hungary's territory.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Mazzini says the countries of the peoples will be defined by the vote of free men, which makes a free popular vote the way boundaries are settled.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Mazzini says the whole nation must legislate directly or indirectly, Kossuth rests every nation's government on its own sovereign will, and Herder was a democrat who held that government should be by the people.

right-to-secede.rationale: Kossuth's Declaration treats the Croatian separation as rebellion and Hungary's territory as indivisible, and Mazzini pressed for a single Italian unity against the federalists; both treat the nation, not a region, as the unit that decides.

sacred-nation.rationale: Mazzini calls the country God's gift and a Temple whose life is immortal, Fichte makes love of fatherland a wish to live on in the nation's eternal life, and Michelet calls nationality the life of the world, and Mickiewicz makes the Polish nation a Christ-like martyr that rises again.

national-rebirth.rationale: Fichte's Addresses call for a wholly new order and a new national education to renew a nation fallen into self-seeking, and Mazzini describes a regenerated Italy rising as a new force.

patriotic-education.rationale: Fichte's whole programme is a national education forming love of the people, Jahn wants national history and language taught in every school, and Michelet calls for a school that teaches the country as a faith.

nation-first.rationale: Mazzini puts duties to humanity before those to country and says working for one's country is working for humanity; Herder approvingly quotes love of humankind above fatherland.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Mazzini says conquests disfigured God's design of nationalities, Fichte says a people that absorbs another of different descent and language confuses itself, and Herder condemns conquest and empire.

political-violence-never.rationale: Mazzini tells an enslaved people to rise and create arms to fight their oppressors, and Kossuth's government raised a levy and fought for independence; the movement accepts armed national struggle.

revolution-justified.rationale: Mazzini founded Young Italy on armed insurrection for unity and a republic, and Kossuth declared Hungary's independence in arms; revolution for national freedom is the movement's characteristic means.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Mazzini says a person must combat for the redemption of the oppressed wherever they suffer, and he and Kossuth urged outside powers to stop foreign armies from crushing a nation's rising.

non-intervention.rationale: Mazzini argues that a one-sided non-intervention abandons peoples to despots and that intervention to stop intervention is right, and Kossuth asks other powers to prevent Russia's armed intervention; both reject a rule against intervening for any reason.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Mazzini's Duties of Man puts duty before rights and says rights exist only as a consequence of duty, and Herder preferred an ideal of humanity to human rights.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Mazzini rejects the theory of interests as a basis of society in favour of duty and sacrifice, and Fichte treats self-seeking as the sickness of the age that destroyed itself.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Mazzini, Fichte and Michelet all ground the nation in a spiritual life above material well-being, and Mazzini says moral improvement and education come before material gain.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Mazzini's creed rests on faith and a duty to God, and Herder held that morality rests on sentiment rather than reasoned theory.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Mazzini says social change comes from education, faith and duty, not material interest, and Fichte makes a new spiritual education the engine of national renewal.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Herder and Mazzini treat each people as an equal with its own mission and no valid ranking, but Fichte says a German can always be superior to the foreigner, so the strands split.

national-mission.rationale: Mazzini, Michelet and Mickiewicz give their own nation a leading role in freeing the others while Herder rejects any favourite people, so adherents are split.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Fichte holds that a people's language stays one language from its beginnings, but Herder says national characters wear away and are recast in time.

culture-before-state.rationale: Fichte makes national education the first task and Herder defends cultural nations without a state, but Mazzini pursued unity by armed political action first, so the sources split.

notes: Searched themes: nation, language, borders, self-determination, secession, minorities, kin abroad, war and conquest, intervention, means of struggle, education, religion, class, property, family, women, government. Herder's Ideas could only be read through scholarship and a poorly scanned translation. Not found in the sources and left blank: minorities and autonomy, immigration, language purism and revival, citizenship, race. Adherents split between the liberal strand (Herder, Mazzini, Kossuth) and the chauvinist strand (Fichte on German superiority) where marked 0. Mazzini's social programme (property, women, republic) is his own and Herder's, not shown shared by the other strands, so it is blank. Deepen pass: read Herder's Ideen (German, Books 9 and 16 to 20), Jahn, Arndt (Der Rhein, Catechism), the Grimms' Sagen preface and Mickiewicz's Księgi; searched nation and territory, language and purism, minorities and mixing, kin abroad, war, religion, martyrs, education, class, consumption, diplomacy and sovereignty. Kossuth's Faneuil Hall speech rejects language as the basis of nationality, which turned the first pass's language answer into a split. Positions found in one thinker only stay blank: Jahn on loanwords, a single state language and uniformed youth, Arndt on the Alsace as a lost territory and on Germans in the Netherlands and Switzerland, Kossuth on secret diplomacy, Herder on colonies and tutelage. Arndt's Geist der Zeit (the archive.org volume found) held no national-question text; Wikisource, the Deutsches Textarchiv and archive.org's German Grimm scans were unusable (cookie gate, or Fraktur OCR) except the Sagen preface.
